reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: Caused by a mosquito-borne flavivirus transmitted mainly by Culex species, with pigs acting as amplifying hosts and wading birds as the natural reservoir
The great majority of infections are silent; only a small fraction progress to clinical encephalitis, but that subset carries high mortality and disability
In India it is a leading cause of acute encephalitis syndrome, occurring in outbreaks in rice-growing and pig-rearing regions and disproportionately affecting children
Classic presentation is fever, headache and altered sensorium progressing over days, often with seizures and a Parkinsonian movement disorder (masked facies, tremor, rigidity)
There is no specific antiviral therapy; care is supportive, centred on seizure control, airway protection and management of raised intracranial pressure
A safe and effective vaccine exists and is incorporated into immunisation programmes in endemic Indian districts, making prevention the cornerstone of control
MRI often shows characteristic bilateral thalamic lesions, sometimes with haemorrhage, which supports the diagnosis
Confirmation relies on detecting JEV-specific IgM in cerebrospinal fluid or serum by capture ELISA
reference.pathophysiology: Japanese encephalitis virus is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus maintained in an enzootic cycle between Culex mosquitoes and amplifying vertebrate hosts, chiefly pigs and water birds. Humans are incidental dead-end hosts. Following a mosquito bite the virus replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing a viraemia that may seed the central nervous system across the blood-brain barrier. Neuronal infection and the accompanying inflammatory response cause neuronal death particularly in the thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebral cortex, accounting for the movement disorders and depressed consciousness seen clinically.
additionalDifferentials: Other arboviral encephalitides (e.g. West Nile, dengue encephalopathy)
additionalInvestigations: JEV-specific IgM capture ELISA in CSF or serum for confirmation
CSF analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly raised protein and normal glucose
MRI brain looking for bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia signal change
EEG to assess for seizure activity and encephalopathic patterns
Investigations to exclude treatable mimics such as HSV PCR and malaria films
redFlags: Rapidly declining consciousness or coma indicating severe encephalitis and need for critical care
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem involvement (abnormal breathing, pupillary changes)
Progressive respiratory compromise requiring airway protection and ventilation
reference.prognosis: Symptomatic encephalitis carries substantial mortality, and a large proportion of survivors are left with lasting neurological or psychiatric sequelae including motor deficits, movement disorders, cognitive impairment and epilepsy. Outcome is worse at the extremes of age and with delayed presentation.
pitfalls: Attributing acute encephalitis syndrome to JE without confirmatory serology and missing treatable causes such as herpes encephalitis
Overlooking the diagnosis outside the classic transmission season or in adults in newly endemic areas
Failing to protect the airway and control seizures early in a deteriorating patient
Neglecting vaccination and vector-control opportunities in endemic districts
management: Supportive intensive care, as no specific antiviral exists, with airway protection and ventilation for depressed consciousness
Seizure control with benzodiazepines and maintenance anticonvulsants
Management of raised intracranial pressure with head positioning, osmotic therapy and neuroprotective measures
Fluid, electrolyte and nutritional support, with treatment of secondary infections
Early rehabilitation through physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy for motor, movement-disorder and cognitive sequelae
Prevention through Japanese encephalitis vaccination in endemic areas alongside mosquito-bite avoidance and vector control
Exclude and empirically treat mimics such as herpes simplex encephalitis with aciclovir and malaria while awaiting confirmation
